---

### 🎯 Practical Learning Objectives

- **Separate** training and test performance and explain why training error is optimistic.
- **Demonstrate** overfitting with a flexible model.
- **Run** k-fold cross-validation and report the mean and spread.

---

## 1. Training Error versus Test Error

```{r load}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
df <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "student_score.csv"))
rmse <- function(y, yhat) sqrt(mean((y - yhat)^2))

set.seed(42)
idx   <- sample(nrow(df), 18)
train <- df[idx, ]; test <- df[-idx, ]
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

---

## 2. Overfitting: More Flexibility Is Not Always Better

We fit polynomials of increasing degree $d$: $\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \dots + \beta_d x^d$.

```{r overfit}
res <- map_dfr(1:8, function(d) {
  m <- lm(Scores ~ poly(Hours, d), data = train)
  tibble(degree = d,
         train_rmse = rmse(train$Scores, fitted(m)),
         test_rmse  = rmse(test$Scores, predict(m, test)))
})
res |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

res |> pivot_longer(-degree, names_to = "set", values_to = "RMSE") |>
  ggplot(aes(degree, RMSE, colour = set)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Training error always falls; test error does not", colour = "")
```

Training error never increases as the model becomes more flexible. Test error stops improving (and here rises again after degree 5): the extra flexibility is fitting noise (**overfitting**). A model that is too simple has high error on both sets (**underfitting**).

> ✏️ **Student Task 1:** Which degree has the lowest test RMSE? Rerun with `set.seed(7)` and a new split. Is the best degree stable?

```{r task1}
# >>> SOLUTION
best <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  i <- sample(nrow(df), 18); tr <- df[i, ]; te <- df[-i, ]
  e <- sapply(1:8, function(d) rmse(te$Scores, predict(lm(Scores ~ poly(Hours, d), data = tr), te)))
  which.min(e)
}
sapply(c(42, 7, 1, 2, 3), best)
# <<< SOLUTION
```

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
On every one of these splits the lowest test RMSE occurs at degree 5, but the gain over the straight line is small (about 0.6 points of RMSE on a test set of only 7 rows), while the training RMSE falls steadily with degree. The data are almost perfectly linear (r = 0.98), so the extra flexibility is mostly fitting noise. Cross-validation (below) uses all 25 rows for testing and favours the straight line, which shows how a single small test set can mislead.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

---

## 3. k-Fold Cross-Validation

Split the data into $k$ folds. Train on $k-1$ folds, test on the remaining fold, and repeat so that every row is used for testing once.

```{r cv}
cv_rmse <- function(k, degree = 1, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  fold <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(df)))
  map_dbl(1:k, function(f) {
    m <- lm(Scores ~ poly(Hours, degree), data = df[fold != f, ])
    rmse(df$Scores[fold == f], predict(m, df[fold == f, ]))
  })
}
cv <- cv_rmse(5)
round(cv, 2)
c(mean = mean(cv), sd = sd(cv))
```

Report the **mean and standard deviation** across folds, not a single number.

> ✏️ **Student Task 2:** Use 5-fold cross-validation to compare degrees 1, 2 and 5. Which degree has the lowest mean CV RMSE?

```{r task2}
# >>> SOLUTION
map_dfr(c(1, 2, 5), function(d) {
  e <- cv_rmse(5, degree = d)
  tibble(degree = d, cv_mean = mean(e), cv_sd = sd(e))
})
# <<< SOLUTION
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 3:** Compute leave-one-out cross-validation (k = number of rows) for the straight-line model and compare with 5-fold.

```{r task3}
# >>> SOLUTION
loo <- cv_rmse(nrow(df))
c(LOOCV = sqrt(mean(loo^2)), fold5 = mean(cv_rmse(5)))
# <<< SOLUTION
```

## 4. Confusion Matrix Revisited

```{r confusion}
heart <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "heart.csv"))
g <- glm(target ~ age + thalach + chol, data = heart, family = binomial)
table(Actual = heart$target, Predicted = as.integer(fitted(g) > 0.5))
```

This matrix uses the **same** data that trained the model, so it is optimistic.

> ✏️ **Student Task 4:** Redo the confusion matrix using a train/test split and report the test accuracy. Explain in two sentences why test accuracy is the honest number.

```{r task4}
# >>> SOLUTION
set.seed(42)
i  <- sample(nrow(heart), floor(0.8 * nrow(heart)))
g2 <- glm(target ~ age + thalach + chol, data = heart[i, ], family = binomial)
p2 <- as.integer(predict(g2, heart[-i, ], type = "response") > 0.5)
table(Actual = heart$target[-i], Predicted = p2)
mean(p2 == heart$target[-i])
# <<< SOLUTION
```

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
Test accuracy is honest because the model never saw those rows during fitting; accuracy on training rows rewards memorisation. Report the test (or cross-validated) accuracy together with the size of the test set, since a few hundred rows give an uncertainty of a few percentage points.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

---

## 5. Summary and Reflection

- Training error is optimistic; evaluate on unseen data.
- Too simple = underfitting; too flexible = overfitting.
- Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate than one split; report mean and SD.

> 🧠 **Reflection:** Explain overfitting in two sentences to a first-year student, using an exam-revision analogy.
